title: The telencephalon is a neuronal substrate for systemic inflammatory responses in teleosts via polyamine metabolism
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

sections.abstract: Systemic inflammation induces neuroimmune responses in the brain resulting in sickness behaviors and fever, which in endotherms engage a complex neuronal circuitry in higher areas of the brain. In ectotherms, only the hypothalamus has been linked to sickness behaviors and behavioral fever. Here, we demonstrate that the telencephalon, a critical region of the teleost brain responsible for higher-order processing, mounts cytokine responses to systemic inflammation in teleosts that are different from those of the hypothalamus. We identify polyamine metabolism as a core response of the teleost telencephalon to systemic inflammation required for behavioral fever. Our work uncovers a previously unrecognized role for the telencephalon and polyamine metabolism in sickness behaviors in teleosts with implications in fish health and conservation.
sections.methods:
Rainbow trout, initially weighing 0.2 grams, were sourced from Trout Lodge (Washington). Fish were maintained at a constant temperature of 16 °C and fed daily with 2% of their body weight using commercial trout diet (Skretting). Feeding was discontinued one day prior to the collection of gut commensal bacteria. Trout (N = 3 per collection group, mean body weight 23±3 g) were euthanized using an overdose of MS-222 in water (Syndel, 200 ppm) according to the University of New Mexico Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee protocol number 22-201239-MC. Animals were then perfused by a cardiac injection of sterile PBS-heparin solution (Sigma Aldrich) to clear any blood from the gut-associated vasculature. Subsequently, the intestines were carefully removed and dissected lengthwise. Following mucus scraping, bacteria were isolated as previously described ( 56 ). The bacterial pellet was then washed three times with a 1% PBS-BSA solution (pH 7.2), resuspended in sterile PBS. The bacterial pellets obtained for each fish were then combined to make one pool prior to injection. The bacterial suspension was adjusted to achieve an optical density (OD) of 0.4 and injected into the caudal vein using 1 ml heparinized syringes.

To irreversibly suppress polyamine synthesis in isolated gut commensals from rainbow trout, we used the inhibitors DFMA (α-difluoromethylarginine) and DFMO (α-difluoromethylornithine) as previously described ( 65 , 124 , 125 ). Pilot experiments were performed to assess the growth kinetics of isolated gut bacteria in the presence of varying concentrations of each pharmacological agent tested independently (1 mM, 0.5 mM, 0.25 mM, 0.1 mM, 0.05 mM, 0.025 mM, 0.01 mM, and a control vehicle (PBS). Gut bacteria were adjusted to an OD of 0.05 in TSB and 150 ul of the suspension were pipetted onto sterile flat-bottom 96-well plates (N = 4/treatment). Plates were incubated at 30 °C under continuous shaking. Optical density was measured every 3 h for 24 h in an iMark microplate reader (Bio-Rad). Next, we evaluated the effects of growing gut bacteria with equimolar concentrations DFMA and DFMO concurrently using the same experimental set-up. These experiments identified the maximum concentration of DFMA and DFMO that could be used without impacting trout gut bacterial growth, which was 0.25 mM each.

The bacterial cultures were therefore incubated with a solution containing 0.25 mM of each DFMA and DFMO in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) at a temperature of 4 °C for a duration of 2 h as previously described. Following the treatment period, bacteria were pelleted through centrifugation at 7,500 g for 20 min at 4 °C. Next, bacterial pellets underwent three separate washes with PBS. After each wash, suspended bacterial cells were again centrifuged at 7,500 g for 20 min at 4 °C to remove any residual DFMA and DFMO. The optical density of the DFMA-DFMO-treated bacterial suspension was adjusted to OD 0.4. This standardized bacterial preparation was then administered to the animals by i.v injection via the caudal vein.

LPS extraction and measurement of LPS levels in trout serum were performed as explained in SI Appendix , Methods .

Juvenile rainbow trout (23 ±3.2 g body weight) were first sedated with MS-222 anesthesia in water (Syndel, 100 ppm). Animals (N = 7/experimental group) were injected i.v with 70 μl of vehicle, isolated commensal bacteria (OD 0.4), LPS or DFMA-DFMO-treated bacteria (OD 0.4) via the caudal vein. After 4 h and 1 d, trout were euthanized by an overdose of 200 ppm MS-222 anesthesia (Syndel). Prior to tissue collection, animals were transcardially perfused with sterile PBS-heparin solution (Sigma Aldrich) prior to tissue collection. The injections comprised 70 μl of either a vehicle, isolated commensal bacteria with OD 0.4, LPS, or bacteria treated with DFMA-DFMO at an OD of 0.4. Trout were euthanized at 4 h and 1 d postinjection by an overdose of MS-222 in water until opercular movement stopped (Syndel). Prior to tissue collection, a sterile PBS-heparin solution (Sigma Aldrich) was used for cardiac perfusion to ensure the removal of blood and maintain tissue integrity. Then, we collected the spleen and five different parts of the brain, including the olfactory bulbs (OB), telencephalon (Tel), hypothalamus (Hyp), optic tectum (OT), and cerebellum (Cer).

To model chronic dysbiosis in trout, (DSS, MP Biomedicals) was employed to induce colitis-like symptoms following the protocol by Ding et al. ( 56 ). This consisted of 250 ul of a 3% DSS solution (by weight/volume in water) oral gavage to the fish for a consecutive period of 10 d. Throughout the duration of the experiment, fish were fed daily 2% of their total body mass.

Total RNA was extracted from dissected tissues (N = 7) using the Trizol method. Tissue lysis was performed through the addition of two tungsten beads to 1.7 mL Eppendorf tubes containing each tissue and Trizol. The mixture was then subjected to vigorous shaking at 30 Hz for 5 min. Next, the homogenates/lysates were collected, and RNA extraction was performed using a standard chloroform/phenol extraction protocol ( 126 ). Total RNA was quantified using a Nanodrop spectrophotometer. For cDNA synthesis, 1 μg of RNA underwent reverse transcription employing the Superscript III First Strand Synthesis System (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Catalog No. 18080051). Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed using the SSOadvanced Universal SYBR Green Supermix (Bio-Rad, Catalog No. 1725270), with the annealing temperature set at 62 °C using specific primers ( SI Appendix , Table S1 ) for the following genes: il-1b, il-6, tnfa, odc1, odc2, samdc1, samdc2 . Changes in gene expression were quantified employing the Pfaffl method using efa1 as the reference gene ( 127 ).

Aseptic techniques were strictly applied as previously described ( 55 , 128 ). The DNA extraction protocol was conducted in line with procedures previously established by Mitchell & Takacs-Vesbach ( 129 ). To amplify the V1-V3 regions of the prokaryotic 16S rDNA, three distinct PCRs were performed on each sample using the designated primers 28F and 519R, as previously detailed ( 56 ). Library construction for sequencing included both negative and positive controls, consistent with established norms within the microbiome research criteria ( 130 , 131 ). Further details are found in SI Appendix , Methods .

Bacterial loads within each sample were quantified via quantitative PCR targeting the 16S rDNA as previously described ( 55 , 132 ). All PCRs were performed in triplicate using primers specific to the V1 to V3 hypervariable regions as previously described ( 56 ) and explained in SI Appendix , Methods .

Microbial sequence data were analyzed using the Quantitative Insights Into Microbial Ecology 2 package (Qiime2, version 2023.7) ( 133 ). The Divisive Amplicon Denoising Algorithm 2 (DADA2) was utilized for partitioning demultiplexed reads into distinct amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) as described ( 134 ). These ASVs were then aligned against the Silva 16S rDNA reference database (version 138) for taxonomic characterization ( 135 ). Before proceeding to in-depth diversity analyses, samples were normalized to a uniform sampling depth of 4,000 reads per sample to ensure comprehensive rarefaction. The ensuing core diversity assessment was conducted while considering both temporal and experimental treatment factors. Using QIIME2, we computed various alpha diversity indices, including Shannon diversity, Chao1 richness, Pielou's evenness index, and Faith’s phylogenetic diversity (PD). Beta diversity analyses (Weighted UniFrac distances) were performed in QIIME2 and principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) plots were visualized by the Qiime2R package in RStudio (version 1.3.959) ( 136 ). To infer the potential functional profiles of the microbial communities, we employed the PICRUSt2 ( 137 ) algorithm in Linux and visualized the outputs in RStudio (version 1.3.959) ( 136 ).

A 1% (w/v) stock solution of Evan’s blue dye was prepared in sterile PBS and subsequently filtered through 0.2 µm sterile filters to ensure purity. For the experimental procedure, 75 µL of the dye, either in the vehicle or mixed with the gut bacteria suspension, was injected into the caudal vein of rainbow trout, with each fish weighing approximately 10 g (±1.35). Fish were then sampled at 4 h and 1 d. Following euthanasia as above, each fish was perfused with a sterile perfusion solution directly through the heart to remove residual blood and the albumin-Evan’s blue complex from the vasculature. Prior to perfusion, the caudal vein and secondary branchial arch veins were incised to facilitate removal of any residual blood. Subsequently, the olfactory bulbs, telencephalon, hypothalamus, optic tectum, and cerebellum were dissected. The weight of each dissected brain part was recorded, and the tissues were immediately immersed in 50% (w/v) trichloroacetic acid (TCA) and preserved on ice as described ( 52 ). Next, the tissues were subjected to a mechanical lysis step consisting of a 5-min shaking at a frequency of 30 Hz. The resulting homogenate was centrifuged at 7500 g for 20 min at 4 °C ( 52 ). The quantification of extravasated Evans Blue in each sample was achieved through colorimetry, comparing the absorbance of the samples to a standard curve generated from a known serial dilution of Evans Blue in 50% TCA at 610 nm ( 53 ). The calculated dye concentrations were then normalized to the weight unit of each sample, allowing for accurate comparative analysis between samples. Values for each brain region were then divided by the baseline values of the vehicle-injected group for the same brain region.

Collected specimens were lysed using 1% Triton X-100 (v/v) (Sigma) as described ( 138 ). The polyamine profile of each sample including putrescine, spermidine, and spermine levels were quantified employing commercially available ELISA kits (MyBioSource) following the manufacturer’s instructions.

Experimental details for behavioral fever assays can be found in SI Appendix , Methods . Each fish was then placed in an annular thermal preference tank (ATPT) for a 24-h behavior analysis period as described ( 33 ). Fish were terminated via cervical dislocations using approved procedures. All efforts were made to minimize animal stress and to ensure that termination procedures were efficiently performed. All procedures were approved by the University of Alberta Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee protocol number AUP0000706.

Behavioral assessments were conducted using high-resolution positional tracking, an infrared Panasonic CCTV color camera (model WV-CP620) equipped with a 2X variable focal lens (model WV-LZ61/2S), and a centrally positioned overhead lighting system. Video recording was achieved using Bandicam software (Bandicam Company). Analyses of recorded videos were performed with Ethovision XT, Version 11 (Noldus, Wageningen, Netherlands). Behavioral parameters quantified included thermal preference, swimming velocity, and the frequency of transitions between thermal zones, as previously described ( 33 ).

To assess the levels of endotoxin in blood serum among various groups, we initially conducted tests for normality using both the F-test and Bartlett’s test. Group differences were evaluated using either unpaired t-tests or one-way ANOVA, with subsequent analysis through Tukey’s post hoc test for specific comparisons. To evaluate bacterial loads, indicated by 16S gene copy numbers in different tissues, data underwent checks for normal distribution as mentioned. To examine variations across tissues and between groups’ bacterial loads, we utilized both the Brown–Forsythe and Welch’s ANOVA tests; the same methodology was utilized to analyze the behavioral data. To analyze differences in Shannon diversity indices, we first performed normality tests as mentioned earlier. Due to the nonparametric nature of these data, differences among groups were determined using the Kruskal–Wallis test. In instances of significant disparities, post hoc pairwise analysis was conducted, applying corrections for multiple comparisons. For visual interpretation of Weighted UniFrac distances, Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) plots were used. Significance in clustering differences on these plots between groups was ascertained through multivariate dispersion analysis. All statistical evaluations were performed using GraphPad Prism (version 10.0.3) and RStudio (version 4.2.3), considering a P -value of less than 0.05 as statistically significant.
sections.results:
To investigate brain neuroimmune responses to systemic inflammation we developed two in vivo models in juvenile rainbow trout ( Fig. 1 A ). Model 1, the acute inflammation model, consisted of three treatment groups that were sampled at 4 h postinjection (hpi) and 1 d postinjection (dpi). A vehicle group, a group injected intravenously (i.v) with bacteria isolated from the gut of healthy rainbow trout and a third group which received an i.v injection LPS purified by us from healthy trout gut bacteria ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 A and B ). Because ectotherms are highly refractory to E. coli LPS injection ( 47 – 49 ), it was important to isolate LPS from the native trout gut microbiota instead of using commercial sources. We first measured LPS levels in the serum of trout injected i.v with the isolated bacteria ( Fig. 1 B ). Notably, LPS levels were only elevated in the blood serum of fish injected with gut bacteria at 4 hpi, returning to baseline levels by 1 d ( Fig. 1 B ). Next, we adjusted how much of the commensal LPS we would need to inject to match this value in both models ( Fig. 1 A and B ). In model 2, we induced chronic gut dysbiosis using the well-established, chemically induced colitis model based on dextran sodium sulfate (DSS) gavage as described in the methods section. In both models, we noted reductions in fish locomotion, but no mortalities occurred during any of the experiments.

Previous studies have established that like mammals, the teleost hypothalamus (Hyp) expresses pyrogenic cytokines in response to systemic inflammation or systemic infection ( 28 , 32 , 35 ). However, whether other regions of the teleost brain respond to systemic inflammation is currently unknown. We hypothesized, given the role of the teleost telencephalon (Tel) in higher-order processing, that this region would be part of the neuronal circuitry responding to systemic insults. Thus, we compared the expression of pyrogenic cytokine genes in the Hyp and Tel, as well as three other brain regions: the olfactory bulb (OB), optic tectum (OT), and cerebellum (Cer) in our acute inflammation model 1. As previously reported in the Hyp, il-1b , tnfa , and il-6 expression was significantly higher (twofold to fourfold increase) in commensal-injected and LPS-injected trout 4 hpi ( Fig. 1 D , F , and H ). Expression levels of all cytokines returned to baseline by 1 d for both the commensal and LPS-injected groups in the Hyp ( Fig. 1 D , F , and H ). In the Tel and OT, il-1b and tnfa expression rose twofold and threefold at 4 hpi in both the bacteria-injected compared to controls. Expression levels in the LPS group were also elevated compared to controls but significantly lower than in the bacteria-injected group ( Fig. 1 C and E and SI Appendix , Fig. S1 B and E ). Importantly, differences between the Tel and OT occurred at 1 dpi, when il-1b expression was significantly down-regulated in both bacteria and LPS injected groups in the Tel, but expression levels were identical to the vehicle controls in the OT ( Fig. 1 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S1 B ). Tnfa responses, on the other hand, were similar in the Tel and OT both in magnitude and kinetics. Critically, and in sharp contrast to the Hyp, il-6 expression remained unchanged at all tested timepoints and treatments in both the Tel ( Fig. 1 G ) and the OT ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 H ). The OB showed no changes in il-1b ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 A ) or tnfa ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 D ) expression following injection of gut-derived bacteria or LPS at 4 hpi and 1 dpi. Interestingly, il-6 expression increased in the OB in both treatment groups compared to controls. Unlike the Hyp, the moderate responses detected in the OB (1.5 to 1.7-fold increase) remained elevated at both 4 hpi and 1 dpi ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 G ). The Cer did not exhibit changes in tnfa expression; however, il-1b and il-6 expression increased 1.5-fold compared to controls in the gut bacteria-injected group 4 hpi ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 C , F, and I ), returning to baseline levels by 1 dpi ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 C and I ). Isolated LPS injection caused a small upregulation in il-6 expression (1.2-fold) in the Cer at 4 hpi, which was no longer detectable by 1 dpi ( SI Appendix , Fig. S1 I ). Combined, these findings suggest that brain regions beyond the Hyp participate in pyrogenic cytokine responses to systemic inflammation in teleosts, and that il-6 responses are decoupled from il-1b and tnfa responses in the Tel and OT.

LPS and other systemic inflammation mediators cause breakdown of the blood–brain barrier (BBB) in mammals ( 50 , 51 ). We measured the integrity of the trout BBB in response to the injection of gut-derived bacteria using Evans blue extravasation, a widely used technique to measure BBB permeability ( 52 – 54 ) ( Fig. 1 I and J ). We measured Evans blue extravasation in five different brain regions including olfactory bulb (OB), Tel, Hyp, optic tectum (OT), and cerebellum (Cer). These values were compared to baseline extravasation levels for each corresponding brain region in animals that were i.v injected with vehicle and Evans blue. BBB permeability increased by twofold compared to vehicle controls in all regions examined by 4 hpi ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 C– E ) except for the Tel, where we observed a >3-fold increase in Evans blue extravasation at 4 hpi when compared to baseline levels ( Fig. 1 J ). This increased permeability was transient, with levels dropping back to baseline values by 1 dpi, indicating a temporary disruption of the BBB in the Tel ( Fig. 1 J ). In contrast, other brain regions including the Hyp, showed no significant BBB disruption by 1 d ( Fig. 1 J and SI Appendix , Fig. S2 C– E ). These data indicate that systemic inflammation preferentially breaks down the Tel BBB compared to other brain regions in rainbow trout.

Systemic bacteria transiently and selectively penetrate the trout telencephalon

Our in vivo acute inflammation model revealed that not only the Hyp, but other brain regions, respond differently to systemic inflammation, with the Tel showing particular vulnerability to BBB disruption. We have recently reported that salmonids have a resident bacterial community in their brain at steady state ( 55 ). We therefore wondered whether upon systemic injection of microbiota, bacteria would be able to penetrate the brain. We quantified total bacterial loads in the spleen and five regions of the brain 4 hpi and 1 dpi using 16 s rDNA qPCR. In the Tel, a substantial increase in bacterial loads was observed at 4 hpi with gut commensals. Bacterial presence was transient, as levels at 1 dpi did not differ significantly from baseline measurements ( Fig. 2 A ). Conversely, the bacterial loads in the Hyp, OB, OT, Cer, and the spleen remained unchanged ( Fig. 2 B and SI Appendix , Fig. S3 E– J ). As predicted, the administration of LPS did not change bacterial loads in any tissue sampled at either 4 hpi or 1 dpi ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 E– J ). We next tested another model (model 2) of gut bacterial translocation and systemic inflammation ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 A ). We employed the recently developed DSS-induced colitis in rainbow trout ( 56 ) and 1 d after the last DSS gavage, we collected the same tissues as before except the Hyp ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 A ). Similar to the i.v injection model, we noted significant increases in serum endotoxin levels in DSS-treated compared to vehicle-treated controls ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 B ), but bacterial loads were only significantly higher in the Tel of DSS-treated animals compared to controls, with no other significant changes noted in the other brain regions ( SI Appendix , Fig. S4 C– G ). A caveat of our study was that we did not separately collect the Hyp in model 2 and therefore we do not know at this point whether bacterial levels increased in the Hyp or not in the DSS model. Combined, these experiments indicate that transient and region-specific bacterial translocation occurs in the trout brain during systemic inflammation.

Given that bacteria penetrate the trout Tel, we next sought to evaluate whether shifts in the Tel microbial community occur following i.v bacterial injection using 16S rDNA sequencing. Collected gut bacteria from healthy laboratory rainbow trout were predominantly composed of four bacterial phyla: Tenericutes (72.2%), Proteobacteria (11.2%), Fusobacteria (7.4%), and Firmicutes (7.2%). Further analysis at the family level revealed the bacterial community to consist primarily of eight families: Mycoplasmataceae (72.2%), Fusobacteriaceae (7.2%), Lachnospiraceae (4.9%), Chitinibacteriaceae (3.0%), and Burkholderiaceae (1.9%) ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 A and B ) and were markedly different from the tank water microbial community ( SI Appendix , Fig. S5 A and B ). The predominant bacterial phyla identified in the Tel of control animals included Proteobacteria (37.93%), Tenericutes (27.0%), Actinobacteria (16.5%), and Bacteroidetes (7.9%) mainly composed of Mycoplasmataceae (27.04%), propionibacteriaceae (11.3%), Chitinibacteriace (10.7%), and Shewanellaceae (9.1%) families ( Fig. 2 C and D ). Finally, the bacterial composition in the tank water was markedly different from that observed in the Tel and composed mostly of members of Acidobacteria (29.5%), Bacteroidetes (31.2%), Proteobacteria (17.3%), and Nitrospirae (6.2%) phyla, such as the families Blastocatellia (uncultured family, 26.6%), Microsillaceae (8.1%), Nitrospiraceae (6.2%), and Saprospiraceae (11.4%), indicating a unique microbial community compared to that of the Tel ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 A and B ). Following i.v injection of bacteria, there was an increase in the relative abundance of Tenericutes, Firmicutes, and Fusobacteria, whereas Proteobacteria, Bacteroidetes, and Actinobacteria relative abundance decreased compared to the vehicle group at the 4-h and 1 d time points ( Fig. 2 C ). At the family level, the relative abundance of Mycoplasmataceae, Lachnospiraceae, and Chromobacteriaceae increased at both time points ( Fig. 2 D ). Conversely, the relative abundance of families such as Enterobacteriaceae, Moraxellaceae, and Shewanellaceae diminished at the same intervals ( Fig. 2 D and G ). While the Tel microbial community composition at the 4 hpi and 1 dpi were largely similar, Ruminococcaceae and Streptococcaceae accounted for 10.4% and 7%, respectively, of the overall diversity at 4 hpi whereas they were only 1.3% and 0.3%, respectively, at 1 d. At 1 d, Fusobacteriaceae and Chitinibacteriace relative abundances were 15.4%, and 8.3%, respectively, a much larger percentage than at 4 hpi (0% and 0.1%) ( Fig. 2 D ). The Weighted UniFrac distance between the Tel bacterial community of vehicle-injected group and commensal-injected group was significantly different at 1 d ( Fig. 2 E ). Principal coordinate analysis revealed distinct microbial community compositions between the vehicle and commensal injected groups, with the Tel microbial communities of the injected animals remaining closely clustered ( Fig. 2 F ). Alpha diversity metrics (Shannon diversity, Chao1, and Pielou's evenness) did not show any significant differences in bacteria-injected versus vehicle-injected animals ( SI Appendix , Fig. S5 C– E ).

PICRUSt2 analysis revealed shifts in functional pathways of the Tel microbial community following i.v injection of bacteria. A total of 27 pathways were significantly modulated in the Tel microbial community at 4 h and 1 d compared to vehicle controls. Several polyamine biosynthesis pathways, such as putrescine, spermidine, and spermine biosynthesis were up-regulated at both time points compared to controls ( Fig. 2 H ). Additionally, nucleotide biosynthesis, including adenine and guanine pathways, L-glutamine and L-lysine biosynthesis, and degradation pathways like L-histidine degradation and fatty acid salvage were modulated as a result of the bacterial injection treatment ( Fig. 2 H ). These results indicate that, despite bacterial loads dropping by 1 d, the systemic inflammation in the Tel microbial community composition and its predicted functions has longer-lasting impacts. Combined, these results show that only specific suites of gut systemic bacteria penetrate the Tel of rainbow trout altering its community composition and predict changes in polyamine metabolism in the Tel bacterial community.

Polyamines are polycationic organic molecules with two or more amino groups. Polyamines are universal molecules in nature, produced by archaea, bacteria, and eukaryotes and are involved in fundamental biological processes such as growth, cell proliferation, differentiation, and death ( 57 – 60 ). Importantly, many of the enzymatic pathways that lead to the production of polyamines from their substrates are shared between microorganisms and eukaryotes ( 57 , 61 – 63 ). Given that the Tel microbial composition showed predicted changes in bacterial polyamine synthesis pathways, we next asked whether these shifts had an impact on host polyamine synthesis pathways. Thus, we measured expression levels of four genes encoding for polyamine synthesis enzymes ( odc1 , odc2 , samdc1 , and samdc2 ) in the trout Tel and Hyp ( Fig. 3 A and B ). We observed a marked increase in the expression of odc genes in the Tel, with twofold and threefold elevations at 4 hpi and 1 dpi of gut commensals, respectively ( Fig. 3 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S6 A ). Conversely, a significant decrease in the levels of samdc transcripts was noted in the Tel, with twofold and threefold reductions at 4 hpi and 1 dpi of gut commensals, respectively ( Fig. 3 D and SI Appendix , Fig. S6 C ). LPS injection also resulted in changes of odc and samdc expression in the trout Tel, with similar trends and fold changes as those observed after injection of gut-derived bacteria ( Fig. 3 C and D and SI Appendix , Fig. S6 A and C ). Interestingly, odc and samdc gene expression did not change in the Hyp at any given time point or treatment group ( Fig. 3 E and F and SI Appendix , Fig. S6 B and D ), indicating that host polyamine responses to systemic bacteria are region-specific.

In order to test whether host changes in polyamine synthesis gene expression are dependent on the ability of bacteria to make polyamines, we blocked polyamine metabolism in the microbiota prior to injecting them into the host. We treated isolated gut commensals with the polyamine pathway inhibitors DFMA (α-difluoromethylarginine), an irreversible inhibitor of arginine decarboxylase, and DFMO (α-difluoromethylornithine), an irreversible suicide inhibitor of ornithine decarboxylase ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 A– D ). Since polyamines can be essential for bacterial growth ( 61 – 64 ) we first performed in vitro experiments to establish the highest dose of DFMA and DFMO that would not compromise bacterial growth ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 A to D ). Based on these assays we selected 0.25 mM for each drug for all subsequent in vivo experiments ( Fig. 3 B ). Bacteria were washed three times prior to injection to ensure the removal of DFMA and DFMO ( 65 ). We first assessed whether treated bacteria were still capable of translocating into the trout Tel and found that polyamine synthesis blockade did not impact the ability of bacteria to enter the Tel 4hpi ( SI Appendix , Fig. S3 E– J ). In response to injection of DFMA-DFMO-treated bacteria, trout odc or samdc expression levels did not change in the Tel or Hyp at the time points tested ( Fig. 3 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S6 A– D ). Combined, these results indicate that bacterial-derived polyamines selectively modulate host polyamine synthesis pathways in the Tel but not the Hyp in rainbow trout.

We next asked whether changes in the expression of polyamine synthesis genes in the trout Tel correlated with changes in the Tel polyamine levels. We measured putrescine, spermidine, and spermine levels in telencephalic tissue extracts under the different experimental conditions using ELISA. Systemic injection of gut commensals resulted in a twofold increase in telencephalic putrescine levels at both 4 hpi and 1 dpi ( Fig. 3 G ). Conversely, a sharp decrease in spermidine, and spermine levels was observed in commensal-injected trout, with a threefold to fivefold reduction at both time points ( Fig. 3 H and I ). Putrescine, spermidine, and spermine levels in the Tel of trout injected with DFMA-DFMO-treated bacteria were not different from vehicle controls. ( Fig. 3 G– I ). Additionally, injection of isolated LPS also caused an increased in putrescine levels in the Tel, showing a similar trend to the gut bacteria-injected group with a twofold increase ( Fig. 3 G ). However, isolated LPS did not affect the Tel spermidine and spermine levels at 4 hpi or 1 dpi ( Fig. 3 H and I ). These results indicate that systemic inflammation shifts host polyamine metabolism in the Tel resulting in putrescine accumulation. Furthermore, our data also indicate the downstream reduction of spermidine and spermine levels in the Tel occurs in response to presence of systemic bacteria but not purified LPS, at least at the timepoints tested in our model.

Polyamines play crucial roles in innate immunity in mammals ( 66 – 68 ). We therefore asked whether polyamines from microbiota could drive the expression of pyrogenic cytokines in the trout brain and hypothesized that this may occur in a region-specific manner. We administered DFMA-DFMO-treated or untreated bacteria to animals ( Fig. 4 A ) and measured il-1b , tnfa , and il-6 transcript levels at 4 hpi and 1 dpi. Untreated bacteria augmented the expression of il-1b and tnfa in the Tel 4 hpi. In sharp contrast, DFMA-DFMO-treated bacteria failed to induce any significant changes in the expression levels of these cytokines ( Fig. 4 B and D ). Additionally, the expression pattern of il-6 in the Tel remained consistent across all treatment groups and the vehicle control ( Fig. 4 F ). Conversely, the Hyp, which exhibited no changes in bacterial loads or in the expression of polyamine synthesis enzymes following injection, was agnostic to the ability of bacteria to synthesize polyamines. Bacteria injection, whether treated with DFMA-DFMO or untreated, resulted in an increase in the expression levels of il-1b , tnfa , and il-6 , with fold changes ranging from 2 to 3, 4 hpi ( Fig. 4 C , E , and G ). Subsequently, the expression levels of these cytokines returned to their normal baseline within 1 dpi. These results suggest that polyamines derived from systemic bacteria and/or from the bacteria that penetrate the Tel directly modulate pyrogenic cytokine responses in the Tel but not the Hyp.

Behavioral fever is teleosts has been demonstrated in several models including viral and bacterial infections, killed bacterial challenges, and exposure to inflammatory agents like LPS or zymosan ( 30 , 32 , 33 ). However, whether the presence of microbiota in the systemic compartment induces behavioral fever in teleosts is currently unknown. We utilized a specialized annular thermal preference tank recently developed to document behavioral changes during fish fever ( 33 ) to assess the responses of four experimental groups ( Fig. 4 H ). We observed that both i.v injection of gut commensals and LPS isolated from gut bacteria induced behavioral fever. Both groups reached a peak preferred temperature of 16 °C ( Fig. 4 I– L ). However, fish injected i.v with gut commensals exhibited a more rapid onset of warm-seeking behavior compared to the LPS-injected group ( SI Appendix , Fig. S5 A ). Two lethargy indicators were also evident in the commensal-injected and LPS-injected groups. Both groups displayed a marked decrease in swimming mobility and velocity ( Fig. 4 K and L ). Notably, maximum lethargy induced by systemic commensals occurred 2 h earlier than by LPS ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 A and B ). In contrast, treatment of bacteria with DFMA-DFMO prior to i.v injection prevented the increase in thermal preference and fever-associated lethargy behaviors. These fish showed no significant deviation from those behaviors in the vehicle-injected group ( Fig. 4 I– L ). Across all measured parameters, the response of animals injected with DFMA-DFMO-treated commensals mirrored the behavioral patterns shown in the vehicle-injected group throughout the 24-h study duration ( Fig. 4 I and SI Appendix , Fig. S7 A and B ). Together, these experiments revealed that 1) systemic inflammation induces behavioral fever in trout, and 2) commensal-derived polyamines are necessary to induce behavioral fever in trout under a scenario where systemic inflammation facilitates microbial translocation into the telencephalon.
sections.discussion:
Sickness behaviors and fever are intricate, coordinated neurobehavioral processes that enhance survival rates in vertebrates ( 12 , 29 , 69 – 72 ). As such, the vertebrate brain must sense and respond to peripheral and systemic insults to help the host return to homeostasis. The complex neuronal circuitry and immune mediators involved in mammalian sickness behaviors are fairly well characterized, reaching higher-order brain regions beyond the Hyp ( 9 – 13 ). However, the neuroimmunological basis for sickness behaviors in ectotherms remains poorly understood.

Teleost fish, like other ectotherms, display sickness behaviors in response to infection characterized by reduced locomotor activity, social withdrawal, reduced appetite, and behavioral fever ( 29 , 32 , 33 , 35 ). Until now, the POV of the Hyp has been the only brain region implicated in responses during sickness behaviors and fever in teleosts ( 30 – 32 , 73 , 74 ). We hypothesized that higher-order processing regions of the teleost brain must participate in the neuroimmune response to systemic inflammation.

Here, we present an acute systemic inflammation model in rainbow trout that mimics the presence of leaked microbiota or their products (LPS) in the systemic compartment. Since teleost fish are highly refractory to E. coli LPS injection ( 47 – 49 ), we reasoned that direct injection of commensal bacteria or commensal-derived LPS i.v would be a more biologically relevant model of acute systemic inflammation than commercial LPS sources. In support, both experimental treatments triggered canonical pyrogenic cytokine responses in the Hyp by 4 hpi, as previously demonstrated by others using infection models ( 32 , 33 , 73 ). In contrast, while il-1b and tnfa expression also increased in the Tel, il-6 responses were not induced. Interestingly, and in agreement with the observations in salmon where both the Tel and the OT express EP3, the OT also showed similar responses to those of the Tel, yet il-1b expression was quickly down-regulated in the Tel but not the OT. Further studies are warranted to understand these regional differences, especially at the protein level, in the teleost brain. Our regional pyrogenic cytokine survey also revealed clear differences in il-6 expression patterns in response to systemic inflammation, the OB, Hyp, and Cer being the only three brain regions with significant expression changes, at least at the time points examined in our model. In mammals, IL-6 can have pro- and anti-inflammatory roles in the brain ( 75 – 77 ). When injected systemically or into the brain, IL-6 causes some sickness behaviors in mammals ( 78 ), with unique biological activities compared to IL-1β ( 78 ). For instance, following a high dose of LPS injection, IL-1β knockout mice display reduced fever compared to controls, however, IL-6 knockout mice have normal fever responses ( 79 ). Additionally, IL-6 does not induce septic shock ( 80 , 81 ) and injection of anti-IL-6 directly into the anterior POA suppresses PGE2 ( 82 ) and Cox2 ( 83 ). In teleosts, we know very little about the biological functions of IL-6. However, a study found that trout recombinant IL-6 reduces il-1b and tnfa expression in macrophages in vitro ( 84 ), suggesting that IL-6 responses dampen inflammation in trout. Assuming a similar function in the brain, il-6 expression in the hypothalamus (and to a lesser extent the OB and Cer) would reduce il-1b and tnfa expression creating a negative feedback loop that limits inflammation, whereas in the Tel and the OT, il-1b and tnfa effects should be prolonged. Intriguingly, trout have two fish-specific IL-6 family genes, the ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF-like) and M17 and CNTF-like is highly expressed in the brain ( 85 ). Thus, we cannot rule out that one or both molecules play alternative or complementary functions to canonical IL-6 in the teleost brain. Additionally, expression patterns of il-6 receptor genes may shed light on regional responsiveness to IL-6 in the trout brain.

The BBB becomes leaky in response to systemic inflammation such as LPS injection, a phenomenon well-documented in mammals ( 50 , 51 ). Loss of BBB integrity in response to LPS injection varies across different brain regions in mammals ( 50 ). Similarly, our studies indicate that the teleost BBB vulnerability to systemic inflammation varies among brain regions and that the Tel BBB is particularly susceptible to disruption in rainbow trout. Whether this is due to the unique cellular and molecular composition of the Tel BBB remains open for further investigation. Interestingly, our study surprisingly found that, in rainbow trout, circulatory bacteria transiently penetrate the Tel but not other brain regions under both acute (intravenous injection) and chronic (DSS-induced colitis) conditions. Prior research identified the insular cortex as a critical detector of peripheral inflammation in mice during DSS-induced colitis ( 16 ). However, this study did not explore whether bacterial translocation from the gastrointestinal tract to the bloodstream resulted in consequent bacterial infiltration into the brain. Nonetheless, the rapid and transient increase in bacterial loads observed in the trout Tel suggests a controlled mechanism by which the teleost brain may directly detect or sample changes in blood-borne bacteria. Whereas bacterial presence in the mammalian brain is thought to be a sign of disease ( 86 – 89 ), regulated bacterial incursions may not significantly harm the teleost brain. This hypothetical scenario is supported by the fact that, compared to mammals, the teleost brain harbors a higher number of immune cells under normal conditions ( 90 ) and possesses remarkable regenerative capabilities following injury ( 91 – 95 ).

We have recently reported that the trout brain has a resident bacterial community ( 55 ). Here, we show that significant shifts in microbial community composition occur in the trout Tel following an i.v injection of gut bacteria. Following i.v injection, some bacteria will rapidly be eliminated by the blood immune system. Yet, we noted changes in the telencephalic microbial community 4 hpi that persisted by 1 dpi. We noted expansions of specific taxa such as Ruminococcaceae, Streptococcaceae, and Mycoplasmataceae at 4 hpi, that were mostly undetectable by 1 d indicating a transient colonization. This may be explained by rapid elimination of bacteria by the trout brain's innate immune response or failure to outcompete other resident microbes. In contrast, Fusobacteriaceae and Chitinibacteriace were expanded in the Tel after 1 d, potentially indicating longer-term dysbiosis in the brain following a single systemic inflammation event. We currently do not know how systemic bacteria penetrate the trout Tel, although our data suggest that the greater BBB disruption of the Tel may facilitate bacteria penetration. In support, we recently reported that mature Chinook salmon, where the gut barrier is disrupted, LPS levels increase in circulation and bacterial loads increase in the Tel ( 55 ). Thus, our findings suggest that teleosts may experience shifts in brain microbiomes throughout their lifespan, some associated with physiological and developmental changes, some because of stress, inflammation, or infection.

Polyamines are polycationic compounds produced by eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells via common enzymatic pathways that utilize the same substrates and generate the same end products ( 57 , 62 , 63 , 96 ). In the vertebrate nervous system, polyamines are involved in neurodevelopment, synaptic plasticity, cognition, aging, and behavior ( 97 – 100 ). Importantly, polyamine metabolism and accumulation of putrescine are thought to be a protective biochemical program following brain insults in both mammals and fish ( 101 – 104 ). Our results indicate that specific regions of the trout brain (the Tel), but not others (the Hyp) quickly respond to systemic inflammatory cues by shifting polyamine metabolism. Specifically, we observed an accumulation of putrescine and a decrease in spermidine and spermine levels in the Tel following gut-derived microbiota injection. In support, putrescine was shown to accumulate in the goldfish brain following cold exposure suggesting that this protective response helps fish adapt to environmental changes ( 101 ). We also noted drastic decreases in telencephalic spermine levels following gut-derived microbiota injection. Since spermine inhibits proinflammatory cytokine responses, at least in humans ( 105 ), decreasing spermine levels in the Tel may be an effective mechanism to ensure pyrogen production, a hypothesis that merits further investigation. Additionally, and in contrast with the bacteria-injected trout, we did not detect significant changes in spermidine and spermine levels in the Tel of LPS-injected trout despite the fact that putrescine levels were significantly higher than in controls. These differences may be due to the presence of multiple inflammatory triggers (i.e flagellin, CpGs) and/or the direct penetration of bacteria into the Tel in the bacteria compared to the LPS-injected group. It is also possible that the kinetics of the polyamine response in the Tel of the LPS-injected animals differ from those of the bacteria-injected group and therefore the two time points selected for our readouts did not fully capture spermidine and spermine changes in this treatment group. In any case, these results indicate that behavioral fever responses to circulating LPS are also coupled to some changes in brain polyamine levels, specifically putrescine accumulation. It is intriguing that changes in polyamine metabolism were not evident in the Hyp, reinforcing the notion that compartmentalized responses to systemic inflammation occur in the teleost brain, with the Tel being the focal point of polyamine-mediated responses. Whether polyamine shifts occur in the OT or other brain regions in response to systemic inflammation remains to be determined.

Our study shows that host genes encoding for polyamine synthesis enzymes such as odc and samdc are modulated in the trout brain in response to systemic inflammation. We noted that odc and samdc expression shifts in the trout brain were present both at 4hpi and 1dpi, whereas pyrogenic cytokine gene expression changes mostly occurred at 4hpi. This is not surprising given the broad biological functions of polyamines and the fact that ODC, the rate-limiting enzyme in polyamine biosynthesis, has the shortest half-life of any known enzyme ( 106 ). Thus, rapid and drastic regulation in odc expression is a hallmark of polyamine metabolism homeostasis and polyamines themselves control expression levels of odc via negative feedback regulation ( 107 ). While our study only captured changes in odc and samdc expression at two timepoints and in bulk tissue samples, we predict that the complex neuroimmune responses triggered by systemic insults likely result in very dynamic and cell type-specific gene expression changes in brain odc and samdc .

A caveat of our experimental approach is the pretreatment of bacteria with polyamine inhibitors prior to systemic injection. This approach aimed to selectively block polyamine metabolism in the gut-derived bacteria but not in the host. However, despite careful washing of bacteria prior to injection, it is possible that DFMA/DFMO was released from treated bacterial cells once injected in the host. This effect may be more pronounced in the Tel since bacteria entered this brain region. In this case, our approach could have directly depressed host polyamine metabolism along with its block on bacteria. Thus, although our findings point toward bacterial polyamines as key players of neuroimmune responses and behavioral fever in teleosts, a more cautious and general interpretation of our data is that polyamine metabolism is a core telencephalic response to systemic inflammation that regulates behavioral fever in teleosts. Finally, an important consideration is that DFMA/DFMO treatment may have altered bacterial gene expression as previously reported in the case of Streptococcus pneumoniae , where polyamine metabolism is required for the expression of virulence factors such as capsule biosynthesis and stress response mechanisms ( 108 ). These alterations can influence the pathogenicity of S. pneumoniae by modifying its ability to evade host immune responses and sustain infection ( 108 ). As such, we cannot rule out that treatment with polyamine inhibitors impacted the ability of commensal bacteria to induce sickness behaviors in trout via other mechanisms directly or indirectly regulated by polyamine metabolism.

Polyamine changes in the brain may result in sickness behaviors such as behavioral fever via several mechanisms yet to be determined. First, polyamines are known to cause widespread changes in gene expression of early response genes such as c-fos and c-jun that dictate cell proliferation and differentiation ( 109 – 111 ). Second, polyamines modulate and block ion channels thereby affecting neuronal function ( 112 – 114 ). Third, polyamines are precursors to gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a neurotransmitter that can regulate locomotor function ( 115 , 116 ) in teleosts. Finally, polyamines also control innate immune responses in the brain, at least in mammals ( 66 ). Currently, the role of polyamines in mammalian fever responses remains unclear, with studies pointing to their lack of function as pyretics ( 117 ) or their antipyretic roles ( 118 , 119 ). However, GABA is known to act on the POA regulating body temperature by inhibiting heat production in mammals exposed to thermal increases ( 120 , 121 ). Interestingly, a recent study in human ulcerative colitis (UC) patients detected significant increases in serum N1-acetylspermidine levels, a bacterial-derived polyamine, in patients with moderate to severe UC compared to those with inactive disease ( 122 ) suggesting a role for N1-acetylspermidine in the pathology of UC or as a biomarker for disease severity. This is relevant because 40% of UC patients suffer from low fever of unknown sources ( 123 ) and therefore the possibility that bacterial-derived polyamines mediate this phenomenon is worth further investigation. A critical question of our study is whether the changes in polyamine metabolism detected in the Tel as well as subsequent behavioral fever responses require the incursion of microbiota into the Tel or they occur independently, for instance in response to the presence of bacteria in the systemic compartment. Answering this question would require injecting bacteria mutants that lack the ability to enter the Tel so that we can disentangle systemic versus direct Tel responses.
sections.conclusion: In conclusion, the present study suggests that polyamine metabolism ties immune regulation and behavioral adaptations to inflammation in teleosts, the Tel being the hub for this coordinated response. Yet, many questions remain to be answered, including the exact neuronal inhibitory and excitatory circuitry that connects the POV with the Tel and/or the OT during sickness behaviors and fever in ectotherms. Given that teleosts appear to live in symbiosis with bacteria during healthy states, as evidenced by the presence of blood and brain microbiomes, we postulate that the Tel acts as a major brain sensor of systemic inflammatory states, allowing teleosts to rapidly respond to shifts in blood bacterial levels deviating from homeostasis.
